title: Algorithms
overview: The standard algorithms you must be able to write in pseudocode (Paper 3) and Python (Paper 4): linear and binary search, bubble and insertion sort, and find/insert/delete on stacks, queues, linked lists and binary trees. You also describe ADTs (including graphs and dictionaries), show how one ADT is built from another, and compare algorithms by time and memory using Big O notation.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of linear and binary searching methods.
Show understanding of insertion sort and bubble sort methods.
Show understanding of and use Abstract Data Types (ADT).
Show how it is possible for ADTs to be implemented from another ADT.
Show understanding that different algorithms which perform the same task can be compared by using criteria (e.g. time taken to complete the task and memory used).

definitions.definition: A collection of data together with the operations allowed on it, defined independently of how it is stored.
Checks each element in turn from the start until the item is found or the end of the list is reached.
Repeatedly checks the middle item of a sorted list and discards the half that cannot contain the search item.
Repeatedly compares adjacent items and swaps them if out of order, until a pass makes no swaps.
Takes each item in turn and inserts it into its correct place in the already sorted part of the list.
A LIFO ADT: items are pushed and popped at the same end (the top).
A FIFO ADT: items are added at the rear and removed from the front.
An ADT of nodes, each holding data and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer gives the first node.
A hierarchical ADT in which each node has at most two children (left and right).
An ADT of vertices (nodes) connected by edges, which may be directed and/or weighted.
An ADT of unique keys, each associated with a value that is looked up by its key.
States the order of growth of an algorithm's time or space requirement as the data size n increases, usually for the worst case.

sections.title: Linear search
content: Linear search is the only systematic way to search unordered data: compare every element with the search item, in order, until it matches or the list runs out.
bullets: Starts at the first element and checks each element in sequence.
Stops when the item is found or the end of the array/list is reached (not found).
Does not need the data to be sorted.
Usually makes more comparisons than a binary search: time grows linearly with the number of items, O(n).
Best case 1 comparison (first item); worst case n comparisons (last item or absent).
Return -1 (a rogue value) for 'not found', because 0 is a valid index.

examples.label: Linear search (pseudocode)
examples.content:
// Items[0:99] is a global ARRAY OF INTEGER
FUNCTION LinearSearch(Target : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   FOR Index ← 0 TO 99               // start at the first element
      IF Items[Index] = Target THEN
         RETURN Index                // found: stop searching
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   RETURN -1                         // end of array: not found
ENDFUNCTION

examples.label: Linear search with a not-found result
examples.content:
def linear_search(values, target):
    for index in range(len(values)):   # start at the first item
        if values[index] == target:
            return index               # found: stop early
    return -1                          # end reached: not found

print(linear_search([31, 7, 19, 42, 12], 42))  # 3
print(linear_search([31, 7, 19, 42, 12], 50))  # -1

sections.title: Bubble sort
content: Each pass compares adjacent pairs and swaps any pair in the wrong order, so the largest unsorted item 'bubbles' to the end. The next pass can stop one place earlier, and a flag ends the sort when a pass makes no swaps.
bullets: Compare adjacent items; swap them (via a temporary variable) if out of order.
After each pass the largest remaining item is in its final place, so reduce the range by 1.
Set a Swapped flag to FALSE at the start of every pass; if it is still FALSE at the end, the list is sorted, so stop.
Already sorted: one pass of n − 1 comparisons, O(n). Reversed: n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, O(n²).
Sorts in place: O(1) extra memory (Temp, index and flag only).

examples.label: Bubble sort with a Swapped flag (pseudocode)
examples.content:
// Values[0:5] is a global ARRAY OF INTEGER
PROCEDURE BubbleSort()
   DECLARE Last : INTEGER
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   DECLARE Temp : INTEGER
   DECLARE Swapped : BOOLEAN
   Last ← 5                          // last unsorted position
   REPEAT
      Swapped ← FALSE
      FOR Index ← 0 TO Last - 1
         IF Values[Index] > Values[Index + 1] THEN
            Temp ← Values[Index]
            Values[Index] ← Values[Index + 1]
            Values[Index + 1] ← Temp
            Swapped ← TRUE
         ENDIF
      NEXT Index
      Last ← Last - 1                // largest item now in place
   UNTIL Swapped = FALSE OR Last = 0
ENDPROCEDURE

examples.label: Optimised bubble sort
examples.content:
def bubble_sort(values):
    last = len(values) - 1             # last index still unsorted
    swapped = True
    while swapped and last > 0:
        swapped = False                # reset at the start of each pass
        for index in range(last):
            if values[index] > values[index + 1]:
                temp = values[index]
                values[index] = values[index + 1]
                values[index + 1] = temp
                swapped = True
        last = last - 1                # largest item is now in place
    return values

print(bubble_sort([29, 12, 41, 7, 18, 33]))  # [7, 12, 18, 29, 33, 41]

sections.title: Insertion sort and sort performance
content: The list is treated as a sorted part (at first just item 0) and an unsorted part. Each item (the key) is copied out, larger items in the sorted part shift one place right, and the key drops into the gap. The performance of any sort depends on the initial order of the data, the number of items and the efficiency of the algorithm.
bullets: Start at the second item (index 1); a single item is already sorted.
Copy the key out before shifting, or it is overwritten.
The inner loop needs both conditions: Position >= 0 AND Values[Position] > Key.
Already sorted: 1 comparison per item, n − 1 in total, O(n). Reversed: every item moves to the front, n(n − 1)/2, O(n²).
Each insertion stops as soon as a smaller item is met, so it is usually faster than bubble sort on nearly sorted data.
More items means more work: both sorts are O(n²) in the worst case, so 10 times the data means about 100 times the comparisons.
Sorts in place: O(1) extra memory.

examples.label: Insertion sort (pseudocode)
examples.content:
// Values[0:5] is a global ARRAY OF INTEGER
PROCEDURE InsertionSort()
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   DECLARE Position : INTEGER
   DECLARE Key : INTEGER
   FOR Index ← 1 TO 5
      Key ← Values[Index]            // next item to insert
      Position ← Index - 1
      WHILE Position >= 0 AND Values[Position] > Key
         Values[Position + 1] ← Values[Position]   // shift right
         Position ← Position - 1
      ENDWHILE
      Values[Position + 1] ← Key
   NEXT Index
ENDPROCEDURE

examples.label: Insertion sort with shifting
Pass-by-pass trace of both sorts
How initial order and number of items change the work
examples.content:
Comparisons made by BOTH sorts (bubble sort with the flag):
    n | sorted | reversed
    6 |      5 |        15
   10 |      9 |        45
  100 |     99 |     4,950
 1000 |    999 |   499,500

Sorted: n − 1 comparisons, O(n). Reversed: n(n − 1)/2, O(n²).
Order matters even for the same n: [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1] (one small item at the end) takes bubble sort 15 comparisons but insertion sort only 9.

sections.title: Binary search
content: Binary search starts at the middle of a sorted array. If the middle item is not the target, the half that cannot contain it is discarded by moving the lower or upper bound, and the search repeats on the half that is left.
bullets: Condition: the data must be sorted (ascending or descending) on the search key, in a structure with direct access to the middle item, such as an array.
Find the middle index, Mid ← (Low + High) DIV 2, and compare that item with the search item.
Equal: found. Search item larger: Low ← Mid + 1. Smaller: High ← Mid − 1. The other half is discarded.
Repeat until the item is found, or Low > High (no items left), meaning it is not in the list.
Maximum comparisons ≈ log2 n (exactly ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1), so it is O(log n) in the worst case; best case O(1).
Search time increases as n increases, but logarithmically: doubling n adds only one comparison, whereas linear search time doubles.
Nothing is deleted: only the Low and High pointers move.

examples.label: Binary search (pseudocode)
examples.content:
// Scores[0:10] is a global ARRAY OF INTEGER, sorted ascending
FUNCTION BinarySearch(Target : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Low : INTEGER
   DECLARE High : INTEGER
   DECLARE Mid : INTEGER
   Low ← 0
   High ← 10
   WHILE Low <= High
      Mid ← (Low + High) DIV 2        // middle of the part left
      IF Scores[Mid] = Target THEN
         RETURN Mid
      ENDIF
      IF Scores[Mid] < Target THEN
         Low ← Mid + 1                 // discard the lower half
      ELSE
         High ← Mid - 1                // discard the upper half
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   RETURN -1                           // no items left: not found
ENDFUNCTION

examples.label: Iterative binary search
examples.content:
def binary_search(values, target):     # values must be sorted
    low = 0
    high = len(values) - 1
    while low <= high:                 # items still left to check
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if values[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if values[mid] < target:
            low = mid + 1              # discard the lower half
        else:
            high = mid - 1             # discard the upper half
    return -1

scores = [4, 9, 15, 22, 27, 36, 41, 50, 58, 63, 77]
print(binary_search(scores, 58))  # 8
print(binary_search(scores, 20))  # -1

examples.label: Trace: one hit and one miss

Search for 58

examples.label: Maximum comparisons as n grows
examples.content:
n | linear max | binary max
       10 |        10 |  4
      100 |       100 |  7
    1,000 |     1,000 | 10
   10,000 |    10,000 | 14
1,000,000 | 1,000,000 | 20

Binary maximum = ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 (checked by searching for every value). Multiplying n by 10 adds only 3 or 4 comparisons; doubling n adds 1.

sections.title: ADTs and implementing one ADT from another
content: An ADT is described by what it stores and the operations on it (create, insert, find, delete). The same ADT can be implemented from built-in types (arrays, records, integer pointers) or from another ADT.
bullets: Stack: 1D array plus a top pointer; or a linked list, pushing and popping at the start node.
Queue: 1D array used circularly with front and rear pointers (and a count); or a linked list with front and end pointers; or two stacks.
Linked list: array of records (data + pointer) with a start pointer and a free-list pointer.
Binary tree: array of records (data + left pointer + right pointer) with a root pointer and a free list.
Dictionary: array of key–value records addressed by hashing the key (hash table); or a binary search tree ordered by key.
Array implementation is static: fixed size, so a full stack or queue cannot be extended.
Linked implementation is dynamic: nodes are added or removed as needed and items are relinked by pointers instead of moved, but each node needs extra memory for its pointer.

sections.title: Linked lists (array of records)
content: Each node is a record holding Data and Pointer (the index of the next node). StartPointer holds the first node; unused nodes are chained into a free list starting at FreePointer. Like the coursebook, this note indexes arrays from 0, so NullPointer = -1 marks the end of a list (0 would be a real node).
bullets: Find: start at StartPointer and follow pointers until the item is found or NullPointer is reached; O(n).
Insert: check the free list is not empty, take the node at FreePointer, move FreePointer to the next free node, store the data.
Then find the insertion point with Previous and Current, set the new node's pointer to Current, and point Previous (or StartPointer) at the new node.
Delete: find the node while remembering Previous; point Previous (or StartPointer) at the deleted node's successor.
Return a deleted node to the free list: its pointer ← FreePointer, FreePointer ← its index.
Inserting or deleting at the start is a special case because StartPointer changes.
No data moves when inserting or deleting (only pointers change), but the list can only be searched sequentially.

examples.label: Array-based linked list: find, insert, delete
examples.content:
CONSTANT NullPointer = -1
TYPE ListNode
   DECLARE Data : STRING
   DECLARE Pointer : INTEGER
ENDTYPE
DECLARE List : ARRAY[0:5] OF ListNode
DECLARE StartPointer : INTEGER
DECLARE FreePointer : INTEGER

PROCEDURE InitialiseList()
   DECLARE Index : INTEGER
   StartPointer ← NullPointer         // list is empty
   FreePointer ← 0                    // every node is free
   FOR Index ← 0 TO 4
      List[Index].Pointer ← Index + 1
   NEXT Index
   List[5].Pointer ← NullPointer
ENDPROCEDURE

FUNCTION FindNode(Item : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Current : INTEGER
   Current ← StartPointer
   WHILE Current <> NullPointer AND List[Current].Data <> Item
      Current ← List[Current].Pointer   // follow the pointer
   ENDWHILE
   RETURN Current                       // NullPointer if not found
ENDFUNCTION

PROCEDURE InsertNode(Item : STRING)
   DECLARE NewNode : INTEGER
   DECLARE Current : INTEGER
   DECLARE Previous : INTEGER
   IF FreePointer = NullPointer THEN
      OUTPUT "No free nodes"
   ELSE
      NewNode ← FreePointer             // take the first free node
      FreePointer ← List[NewNode].Pointer
      List[NewNode].Data ← Item
      Previous ← NullPointer
      Current ← StartPointer
      WHILE Current <> NullPointer AND List[Current].Data < Item
         Previous ← Current
         Current ← List[Current].Pointer
      ENDWHILE
      List[NewNode].Pointer ← Current
      IF Previous = NullPointer THEN
         StartPointer ← NewNode         // new first node
      ELSE
         List[Previous].Pointer ← NewNode
      ENDIF
   ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE DeleteNode(Item : STRING)
   DECLARE Current : INTEGER
   DECLARE Previous : INTEGER
   Previous ← NullPointer
   Current ← StartPointer
   WHILE Current <> NullPointer AND List[Current].Data <> Item
      Previous ← Current
      Current ← List[Current].Pointer
   ENDWHILE
   IF Current <> NullPointer THEN
      IF Previous = NullPointer THEN
         StartPointer ← List[Current].Pointer
      ELSE
         List[Previous].Pointer ← List[Current].Pointer
      ENDIF
      List[Current].Pointer ← FreePointer   // back to the free list
      FreePointer ← Current
   ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

examples.label: Trace: four inserts and one delete
examples.content:
Start: StartPointer = -1, FreePointer = 0, pointers 0→1→2→3→4→5→-1 (all free).

After InsertNode M, C, T, F (each takes the next free node 0, 1, 2, 3):
Index | Data | Pointer
  0   | M    |  2
  1   | C    |  3
  2   | T    | -1
  3   | F    |  0
  4   |      |  5
  5   |      | -1
StartPointer = 1, FreePointer = 4. Following the pointers gives C → F → M → T.

DeleteNode C: C is the first node, so StartPointer ← 3 (F). Node 1 goes back on the free list: List[1].Pointer ← 4, FreePointer ← 1.
FindNode T returns 2; FindNode C now returns -1.

examples.label: The same linked list in Python (parallel arrays)
examples.content:
NULL = -1
data = [""] * 6
pointer = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, NULL]        # free list links every node
start = NULL
free = 0

def find(item):
    current = start
    while current != NULL and data[current] != item:
        current = pointer[current]
    return current                     # NULL if not found

def insert(item):                      # keeps the list in order
    global start, free
    if free == NULL:
        return False                   # no free node left
    new = free
    free = pointer[free]
    data[new] = item
    previous, current = NULL, start
    while current != NULL and data[current] < item:
        previous, current = current, pointer[current]
    pointer[new] = current
    if previous == NULL:
        start = new                    # new first node
    else:
        pointer[previous] = new
    return True

def delete(item):
    global start, free
    previous, current = NULL, start
    while current != NULL and data[current] != item:
        previous, current = current, pointer[current]
    if current == NULL:
        return False
    if previous == NULL:
        start = pointer[current]
    else:
        pointer[previous] = pointer[current]
    pointer[current] = free            # node goes back on the free list
    free = current
    return True

for word in ["M", "C", "T", "F"]:
    insert(word)
print(start, free, pointer)  # 1 4 [2, 3, -1, 0, 5, -1]
delete("C")
print(start, free, pointer)  # 3 1 [2, 4, -1, 0, 5, -1]
print(find("T"), find("C"))  # 2 -1

sections.title: Binary trees
content: The top node is the root, nodes with no children are leaves, and each node has a left and a right subtree. In an ordered binary tree (binary search tree) smaller items go in the left subtree and larger items in the right, so a search follows one branch per level. The syllabus requires find and insert for binary trees, not delete.
bullets: Array implementation: records with Data, LeftPointer and RightPointer; a RootPointer; free nodes linked into a free list; -1 = null.
Find: start at the root; go left if the item is smaller, right if larger; stop when found or a null pointer is reached.
Insert: take a free node, then follow branches from the root until a null pointer and attach the new node there as a leaf.
Remember the last node visited and which way you turned, so the correct pointer (left or right) is updated.
Existing nodes never move on insertion; only one pointer changes.
Balanced tree: find and insert are O(log n). Items added in sorted order give a skewed tree like a linked list: O(n).

examples.label: Array-based binary tree: insert and find
examples.content:
CONSTANT NullPointer = -1
TYPE TreeNode
   DECLARE Data : STRING
   DECLARE LeftPointer : INTEGER
   DECLARE RightPointer : INTEGER
ENDTYPE
DECLARE Tree : ARRAY[0:6] OF TreeNode
DECLARE RootPointer : INTEGER
DECLARE FreePointer : INTEGER   // free nodes linked by LeftPointer

PROCEDURE InsertTreeNode(Item : STRING)
   DECLARE NewNode : INTEGER
   DECLARE Current : INTEGER
   DECLARE Previous : INTEGER
   DECLARE WentLeft : BOOLEAN
   IF FreePointer <> NullPointer THEN
      NewNode ← FreePointer
      FreePointer ← Tree[FreePointer].LeftPointer
      Tree[NewNode].Data ← Item
      Tree[NewNode].LeftPointer ← NullPointer
      Tree[NewNode].RightPointer ← NullPointer
      IF RootPointer = NullPointer THEN
         RootPointer ← NewNode          // first node is the root
      ELSE
         Current ← RootPointer
         WHILE Current <> NullPointer   // go down to a leaf
            Previous ← Current
            IF Item < Tree[Current].Data THEN
               WentLeft ← TRUE
               Current ← Tree[Current].LeftPointer
            ELSE
               WentLeft ← FALSE
               Current ← Tree[Current].RightPointer
            ENDIF
         ENDWHILE
         IF WentLeft = TRUE THEN
            Tree[Previous].LeftPointer ← NewNode
         ELSE
            Tree[Previous].RightPointer ← NewNode
         ENDIF
      ENDIF
   ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

FUNCTION FindTreeNode(Item : STRING) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Current : INTEGER
   Current ← RootPointer
   WHILE Current <> NullPointer AND Tree[Current].Data <> Item
      IF Item < Tree[Current].Data THEN
         Current ← Tree[Current].LeftPointer
      ELSE
         Current ← Tree[Current].RightPointer
      ENDIF
   ENDWHILE
   RETURN Current                       // NullPointer if not found
ENDFUNCTION

Find Q: K (right) → R (left) → M (right) → null pointer, returns -1.

sections.title: Stacks and queues
content: A stack is LIFO (last in, first out, also called FILO): items are pushed and popped at the same end, so it needs one movable pointer (top). A queue is FIFO: items are added at the rear and removed from the front, so it needs two movable pointers. Both vary in length as items are added and removed. In an array, a queue is made circular: a pointer that passes the last element wraps round to 0.
bullets: Push: check the stack is not full (overflow); increment TopPointer; store the item.
Pop: check the stack is not empty (underflow); read the item at TopPointer; decrement TopPointer.
Enqueue: check Count < MaxSize; RearPointer ← (RearPointer + 1) MOD MaxSize; store the item; add 1 to Count.
Dequeue: check Count > 0; read the item at FrontPointer; move FrontPointer on with MOD; subtract 1 from Count.
Uses of a stack: procedure calls (return addresses), recursion, interrupt handling, evaluating Reverse Polish expressions, implementing other ADTs.
Uses of a queue: print queues, keyboard/data buffers, process scheduling.
Queue from two stacks: enqueue pushes onto stack 1; dequeue pops from stack 2, first refilling it (if empty) by popping every item from stack 1, which reverses them into FIFO order.

examples.label: Array stack and circular queue (pseudocode)
examples.content:
CONSTANT MaxSize = 5
DECLARE Stack : ARRAY[0:4] OF STRING
DECLARE TopPointer : INTEGER     // -1 when empty
DECLARE Queue : ARRAY[0:4] OF STRING
DECLARE FrontPointer : INTEGER   // starts at 0
DECLARE RearPointer : INTEGER    // starts at -1
DECLARE Count : INTEGER          // starts at 0

PROCEDURE Push(Item : STRING)
   IF TopPointer = MaxSize - 1 THEN
      OUTPUT "Stack full"          // overflow
   ELSE
      TopPointer ← TopPointer + 1
      Stack[TopPointer] ← Item
   ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

FUNCTION Pop() RETURNS STRING
   DECLARE Item : STRING
   Item ← ""
   IF TopPointer = -1 THEN
      OUTPUT "Stack empty"         // underflow
   ELSE
      Item ← Stack[TopPointer]
      TopPointer ← TopPointer - 1
   ENDIF
   RETURN Item
ENDFUNCTION

PROCEDURE Enqueue(Item : STRING)
   IF Count = MaxSize THEN
      OUTPUT "Queue full"
   ELSE
      RearPointer ← (RearPointer + 1) MOD MaxSize   // wrap round
      Queue[RearPointer] ← Item
      Count ← Count + 1
   ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

FUNCTION Dequeue() RETURNS STRING
   DECLARE Item : STRING
   Item ← ""
   IF Count = 0 THEN
      OUTPUT "Queue empty"
   ELSE
      Item ← Queue[FrontPointer]
      FrontPointer ← (FrontPointer + 1) MOD MaxSize
      Count ← Count - 1
   ENDIF
   RETURN Item
ENDFUNCTION

examples.label: Trace: circular queue wrap-round
examples.content:
MaxSize = 5, Front 0, Rear -1, Count 0.
Enqueue A, B, C, D, E → Front 0, Rear 4, Count 5.
Dequeue, Dequeue → returns A then B; Front 2, Count 3.
Enqueue F → Rear (4 + 1) MOD 5 = 0 (wrap round); Enqueue G → Rear 1; Count 5.
Enqueue H → "Queue full".
Array: [F, G, C, D, E] with Front 2, Rear 1.

sections.title: Graphs
content: A graph is an ADT that records relationships: vertices (nodes) joined by edges (arcs). Any vertex can connect to any number of others, which a list or tree cannot represent. You must describe and justify graphs; you will not be asked to write graph code.
bullets: Vertices represent objects (towns, computers, people); edges represent the connections between pairs of vertices.
Weighted (labelled) edges carry a value such as distance, time or cost.
Directed edges work one way only; undirected edges work both ways.
Two vertices joined by an edge are neighbours; a path is a route along edges and may pass through other vertices.
Stored as an adjacency matrix (one row and column per vertex holding 1/0 or the weight) or an adjacency list (each vertex lists only its neighbours).
Justify a graph by linking each feature to the situation: vertices = the places, weights = the distances, directions = one-way routes; shortest-path algorithms (Dijkstra, A*) can then be applied.

sections.title: Dictionaries
content: A dictionary stores key–value pairs: a unique key (such as a product code) is used to look up its value (such as the stock level). It is usually implemented as a hash table: the key is hashed into an array index, so the value is reached by direct access instead of a search. Python's dict is a built-in dictionary.
bullets: Operations: add a pair, look up a value by its key, update a value, delete a pair.
Keys must be unique; values need not be.
From built-in types: TYPE Entry (Key, Value) records in an ARRAY, placed by hashing the key; a collision (two keys, same index) is resolved, e.g. by using the next free slot.
Average look-up is O(1), independent of the number of pairs.

examples.label: Dictionary operations
examples.content:
stock = {"pen": 40, "ruler": 12}       # key -> value
stock["glue"] = 25                     # insert a new pair
stock["pen"] = stock["pen"] - 5        # look up and update by key
del stock["ruler"]                     # delete a pair
print(stock)  # {'pen': 35, 'glue': 25}
print("ruler" in stock)  # False

sections.title: Comparing algorithms: Big O notation
content: Algorithms that do the same task are compared by the time taken and the memory used as the data size n grows. Big O gives the order of growth, normally for the worst case: keep only the dominant term and ignore constants, so 3n² + 5n + 2 steps is O(n²). Time complexity counts steps; space complexity measures the memory needed.
bullets: O(1) constant: same time whatever n is, e.g. push, pop, reading an array element by index.
O(log n) logarithmic: the data is halved each step, e.g. binary search; time rises by one step each time n doubles (linearly as n rises exponentially).
O(n) linear: time proportional to n, e.g. linear search or a single loop over the data.
O(n log n): e.g. merge sort, which splits the data log n times and handles all n items at each level.
O(n²) polynomial: nested loops over the data, e.g. bubble and insertion sort in the worst case.
O(2ⁿ) exponential: time doubles for each extra item, e.g. recursive Fibonacci; impractical for large n.
Space: bubble and insertion sort use O(1) extra memory; an ADT holding n items needs O(n) space.

examples.label: Growth of each order for n = 16 and n = 32
examples.content:
n | log2 n | n log2 n |    n² |           2ⁿ
 16 |      4 |       64 |   256 |       65,536
 32 |      5 |      160 | 1,024 | 4,294,967,296

Doubling n adds 1 step for O(log n), doubles O(n), quadruples O(n²) and squares 2ⁿ.

rows: Linked list find / ordered insert / delete

diagram.title: Binary search process
nodes: Item at Mid = target? Found: return Mid
Target larger: Low ← Mid + 1; smaller: High ← Mid − 1
Repeat while Low <= High; otherwise return -1 (not found)

analysisChains.title: Linear or binary search?
steps: Binary search needs the data sorted first; sorting with bubble or insertion sort costs up to O(n²)
Linear search works on unsorted data with no preparation and needs at most n comparisons
Once sorted, binary search needs at most ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 comparisons: 20 for a million items against up to a million
So the sorting cost is repaid only if the data is already sorted, kept sorted, or searched many times
analysisChains.evaluation: Linear search suits small or unsorted lists searched once; binary search is far faster for large sorted data searched repeatedly.

analysisChains.title: Why initial order changes sort performance
steps: Insertion sort stops each insertion as soon as it meets a smaller item
On sorted data each key needs one comparison: n − 1 in total (O(n))
On reversed data every key moves to the front: n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, 499,500 for 1,000 items (O(n²))
Bubble sort's flag only helps if a whole pass has no swaps; one small item at the end still forces n − 1 passes (15 comparisons against insertion sort's 9 for [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1])
analysisChains.evaluation: Both sorts are O(n²) worst case with O(1) space, so they suit small data sets; insertion sort is usually the better choice when the data is nearly sorted.

analysisChains.title: Justifying a graph for a delivery firm
steps: Depots and customers become vertices; roads between them become edges
Each edge is weighted with the distance or travel time
Each place connects to many others, which a list or tree cannot model; a shortest-path algorithm can then plan routes
analysisChains.evaluation: A weighted, directed graph fits the road network; an adjacency list saves memory when most places connect to only a few others.

examTips: Binary search condition: write 'the data must be sorted/ordered'. For its performance say 'maximum comparisons grow as log2 n, so time increases less rapidly than linear search'.

Marks in search and sort code go for each step: initialise bounds or flags, the loop condition, the comparison, the swap/shift or bound update (Mid + 1, Mid − 1), and returning or outputting found / not found.
In ADT code the full/empty check (or free list not null) is a mark on its own: test it before any pointer changes.
When describing a stack or queue, give LIFO/FIFO, same end/different ends and one/two pointers as separate points.
For 'performance of a sort depends on…' give both the initial order of the data and the number of items, with best and worst cases.
In a trace table, show the array or pointers after each pass or operation, not just the final result.
commonMistakes: Setting Low ← Mid or High ← Mid, so the range may never shrink and the loop never ends.
Applying binary search to unsorted data.
Not resetting Swapped to FALSE at the start of each bubble-sort pass.
Starting insertion sort at index 0, or overwriting the key before the items are shifted.
Forgetting the special case of the first node in a linked list, where StartPointer must change.
Deleting a linked-list node without returning it to the free list, so the space is lost.
Forgetting wrap-round (MOD MaxSize) in a circular queue.
Claiming every binary tree search is O(log n); a skewed tree is O(n).
Writing graph code when the question asks only to describe or justify a graph.

quickRecall.question: What condition must hold before a binary search?
quickRecall.answer: The data must be sorted on the search key.

quickRecall.question: Maximum comparisons for a binary search of 1,000 items?
Two factors that affect the performance of a sorting routine?
quickRecall.answer: The initial order of the data and the number of data items.

quickRecall.question: Best-case time of insertion sort and when it happens?
quickRecall.answer: O(n), when the data is already sorted.

quickRecall.question: What does the Swapped flag do in bubble sort?
quickRecall.answer: If a pass makes no swaps the list is sorted, so the sort stops early.

quickRecall.question: How many pointers do a stack and a queue need?
quickRecall.answer: Stack one (top); queue two (front and rear).

quickRecall.question: How is a queue built from two stacks?
quickRecall.answer: Push new items onto stack 1; dequeue pops stack 2, refilled from stack 1 when empty, which reverses the order to FIFO.

quickRecall.question: What value marks a null pointer in a 0-indexed array linked list?
quickRecall.answer: -1, because 0 is a valid node index.

quickRecall.question: What happens to a deleted linked-list node?
quickRecall.answer: It is added to the front of the free list.

quickRecall.question: Name two key features of a graph.
quickRecall.answer: Vertices joined by edges; edges may be weighted and/or directed.

quickRecall.question: How is a dictionary normally implemented?
quickRecall.answer: As a hash table: each key is hashed to an array index.

quickRecall.question: Order of 5n² + 3n + 7?
quickRecall.answer: O(n²): keep the dominant term, drop constants.
